summary: This specification updates RFC 5545 by adding iCalendar properties and components that are useful to event publishers and in social networking. It also defines a STRUCTURED-DATA property so data directly relevant to an event or task can be included with the calendar data.

eli5.summary: A calendar entry usually holds just time and place. This document adds more fields, like extra details for events people advertise, so calendars can carry richer information.

questions: what is the icalendar participant component
what does rfc 9073 add to icalendar
subtitle: New iCalendar components and properties that let event publishers attach participants, locations, resources and rich data to an event.

tldr.problem: iCalendar (RFC 5545) has no standard way to point to outside information about an event, such as who is performing, where to park, or a rich-text description. People stuffed links into the description or invented nonstandard properties.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9073 adds three components (PARTICIPANT, VLOCATION, VRESOURCE), six properties (including STRUCTURED-DATA and STYLED-DESCRIPTION) and three parameters (ORDER, SCHEMA, DERIVED), so typed references and structured data can travel inside the calendar data.
tldr.outcome: Clients, servers and publishers get a common, registered vocabulary for event metadata. The RFC also warns that following links and revealing participant locations carry security and privacy risks.

today: RFC 9073 is a Proposed Standard from August 2021 that updates RFC 5545. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion RFC 9074 reuses its VLOCATION component for location-based alarms.

sections.title: Why iCalendar Needed More
sections.content:
RFC 5545 defines iCalendar, the common format for calendar data. RFC 9073 says it lacks useful methods for referencing additional, external information about calendar components, and has no standard way to give rich-text descriptions or metadata for an event.

Current practice was to embed such information as links in the description, or to add nonstandard properties. RFC 9073 updates RFC 5545 with properties and components for this, so the information can move between clients, between client and server, and between servers. Formats such as vCard (RFC 6350) are expected to be most useful to receivers, since they can be reused in other applications such as address books.

A notable design choice: earlier extensions mostly added properties or parameters, partly because iCalendar libraries had trouble with components nested deeper than RFC 5545 defines. This RFC deliberately defines components instead, which fits the way XML and JSON handle such structures and leaves room for extra properties inside them.
sections.eli5: Calendars could only hold the basics, so people scribbled extra notes in the margin. This document gives those notes proper boxes with labels.

sections.title: Typed References and Use Cases
sections.content:
The new pieces can all point to external metadata. Because each reference carries type information, clients and servers can find interesting references and use them, for instance to index events or to show related information. The RFC adds that clients should exercise caution in following references to external data.

The existing LOCATION property is a single unstructured text value, which is inadequate when an address, region, country or postal code is wanted. With the VLOCATION component, rich information about several locations (parking, nearby restaurants, the venue) can be carried in a STRUCTURED-DATA property, and servers can use it to index events by geographic location.

The PARTICIPANT component covers organizers, sponsors, and the active and inactive participants of an event, such as a school team and the parents. The RFC gives three scenarios:

  • Piano concert: a published event with a performer pointing to vCard data, plus parking, subway stations, the venue and sponsors.
  • Itineraries: references to businesses at airports and to car hire at the destination.
  • Reserving facilities: a meeting with attendees in different places, where room size and equipment depend on who is actually in the room.
sections.eli5: Imagine an invitation to a concert. Besides the time, you also want to know who is playing, where to park and who paid for it. These new pieces hold exactly that.

sections.title: New Property Parameters
sections.content:
Three parameters are added.

  • ORDER gives the relative order of instances of a property. Its value MUST be an integer of 1 or more, with 1 first. With no ORDER, an instance is ordered last, equal values form an unordered group, and it MUST NOT be used on a property that does not allow multiple instances. An example use is ORDER=1 for the principal performer.
  • SCHEMA holds a quoted URI naming the schema of a STRUCTURED-DATA value. It SHOULD be given on those properties, and supplements the media type in FMTTYPE.
  • DERIVED is TRUE or FALSE (default FALSE). When TRUE, the value was derived from other properties and clients MUST NOT update it. For instance an HTML STYLED-DESCRIPTION may be derived from an RTF one.
sections.eli5: ORDER is the numbered line-up of who goes first. SCHEMA says what kind of form the extra data is written on. DERIVED says 'this is a copy, do not edit it'.

sections.title: New Properties
sections.content:
Six properties are defined, all registered with IANA.

  • LOCATION-TYPE says what kind of location a VLOCATION is (for example a venue or parking). Values come from RFC 4589, and several may be given.
  • PARTICIPANT-TYPE MUST appear once in each PARTICIPANT and takes values such as ACTIVE, SPONSOR or PERFORMER.
  • RESOURCE-TYPE classifies a VRESOURCE with values such as ROOM and PROJECTOR.
  • CALENDAR-ADDRESS gives a calendar user address for a participant. If an ATTENDEE has the same value, the participant is schedulable.
  • STYLED-DESCRIPTION carries one or more rich-text descriptions (for example HTML), as inline TEXT or as a URI link. If several appear, exactly one MUST lack DERIVED or have it FALSE, and all others MUST have DERIVED=TRUE. The plain DESCRIPTION should be absent or a plain-text rendering.
  • STRUCTURED-DATA carries ancillary data in a structured format, inline as TEXT or BINARY, or by link as a URI. The RFC prefers reusing existing schemas (it mentions schema.org) over defining new iCalendar properties for each event type. FMTTYPE and SCHEMA MUST be present for text or inline binary content.

Why not just use ATTACH? It cannot carry a TEXT value, attachments are often treated as opaque, and some implementations strip attachments and replace them with a link. Extending it with a new value type would likely cause interoperability problems.
sections.eli5: Each new property is a labelled sticker: what kind of place, what kind of person, what kind of gear, a fancy description, and a free-form box for extra details.

sections.title: New Components
sections.content:
Three new components can be nested inside VEVENT, VTODO, VJOURNAL and VFREEBUSY. The first two can also contain VLOCATION and VRESOURCE in turn.

  • PARTICIPANT describes someone or something taking part, such as a team, the spectators or the musicians. It requires PARTICIPANT-TYPE and UID, and can refer to a vCard through STRUCTURED-DATA. A PRIORITY orders participants with the same type.
  • VLOCATION gives detail about a venue or related services such as parking, dining or stations. It requires a UID.
  • VRESOURCE describes things an entry needs, such as rooms, projectors and conferencing. It requires a UID.

A participant is schedulable if it has a CALENDAR-ADDRESS equal to an ATTENDEE value. For backwards compatibility the ATTENDEE property MUST still carry the scheduling parameters. A participant can also hold things like the SEQUENCE and DTSTAMP of replies, or a location that helps pick meeting times across time zones.
sections.eli5: A component is a little folder you tuck inside an event. There is a folder for people, one for places and one for equipment.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows a concert event holding a sponsor and a performer as PARTICIPANTs (each pointing to a vCard by URI) and two VLOCATIONs, one for the venue and one for its parking. A second example is a meeting where one attendee is remote: a PARTICIPANT of type ACTIVE with a LOCATION of 'At home'.

The RFC's own STRUCTURED-DATA example embeds a schema.org SportsEvent as JSON-LD text, with FMTTYPE=application/ld+json and a SCHEMA URI. It names a home team and an away team.
sections.eli5: The examples show a concert invitation with a sponsor, a pianist, a venue and a parking lot all listed in tidy boxes.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC points at RFC 3986 for URI risks and says clients SHOULD NOT follow URIs and fetch content automatically, only at the explicit request of the user. Fetching reveals IP and so generally location information, and a malicious calendar with many URIs could become an amplification vector for denial of service. Implementations should limit automatic fetching and keep fetches to well-known ports and allowed protocols, generally HTTP/HTTPS.

STRUCTURED-DATA can be abused with very large values or with recurring events carrying many overrides. Agents should set limits on storage size and instance counts, and servers SHOULD check it for malicious content and remove the property if found. HTML content brings its own issues.

A LOCATION inside a PARTICIPANT reveals where a person will be at a given time. User agents MUST NOT broadcast it without the express permission of those participants, and the RFC notes it could enable targeted attacks. Even ORDER may expose the organizer's view of who matters most.
sections.eli5: Do not open every link in an invitation without asking, and never tell everyone where a person will be unless they said yes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC adds the six properties, three parameters and three components to the iCalendar registries from RFC 5545. It also creates two new registries, for participant types and resource types, with initial contents matching the values listed above.

New tokens are assigned after Expert Review. Tokens should not be specific to a country, region, organization or company, and must be well defined and widely recognized. Tokens MUST also follow the character set restrictions for XML Names.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of allowed labels, and new labels need a reviewer to say yes first.

items.label: Active
items.desc: Taking an active role, such as a team member.

items.label: Inactive
items.desc: Taking an inactive role, such as an audience member.

items.label: Sponsor
items.desc: A sponsor of the event; ORDER may rank several.

items.label: Planner contact
items.desc: Contact for the event planner or organizer.

items.label: Performer
items.desc: A performer such as the soloist or accompanist.
